title: Rules, rights and duties at school
subject: CIVICS

authority.note: Curriculum V2 draft. Requires exact-revision human review; not approved, not published.

objectives.statement: Name a rule at home or school and say how it keeps people safe, healthy or fair.
Tell a right (something every child should have) from a duty (something we should do), with one school example of each.

content.body:
Musu and Kollie both want the ball. They push each other. The ball rolls toward the road.

What should they do? Today we learn about **rules**, **rights** and **duties**.

accessibility.textAlternative: A short story: two children push over a ball, and the ball rolls toward the road.

offline.fallback: The teacher can tell the story without the picture.

content.body:
Today we will:

1. Name a rule and say how it keeps us safe or fair.
2. Tell a right from a duty.

accessibility.textAlternative: Two goals: naming a rule and why it helps, and telling a right from a duty.

offline.fallback: The teacher reads the goals aloud.

content.body: Your teacher reads: *Fatu walked to the market with her mother. They bought rice.*

feedback.correct: Yes! Fatu went with her mother.
feedback.incorrect: Listen again: Fatu went with her mother.

optionFeedback: Yes! Fatu went with her mother.
Listen again: Fatu went with her mother.

items.prompt: Where do children go to learn to read?

feedback.correct: Yes! We learn to read at school.
feedback.incorrect: We buy food at the market. We learn to read at school.

optionFeedback: We buy food at the market. We learn to read at school.
Yes! We learn to read at school.

accessibility.textAlternative: A two-sentence story about Fatu and two spoken questions with two answers each.

offline.fallback: The teacher can ask the questions aloud.

content.body:
A **rule** tells us what to do or not do.

Rules help in two ways:

- They keep us **safe**.
- They help us be **fair**.
keyPoints: Walk near the road: it keeps us safe.
Take turns with the ball: it is fair.

accessibility.textAlternative: A rule tells us what to do. Rules keep us safe and help us be fair, with two examples.

offline.fallback: The teacher can act out both examples.

content.body: Back to Musu, Kollie and the ball. Tap to see what a rule can do.

steps.label: The problem
steps.description: They push, and the ball rolls to the road.

steps.label: Safe rule
steps.description: Do not run into the road. Ask a grown-up to get the ball.

steps.label: Fair rule
steps.description: Take turns. Musu kicks first, then Kollie.

steps.label: Why
steps.description: Now nobody gets hurt, and both children play.

accessibility.textAlternative: Four steps: the problem, a safety rule, a fairness rule, and why the rules help.

offline.fallback: The teacher can tell each step aloud.

content.body:
A **right** is something every child should have.
Every child has a right to be safe and to go to school.

A **duty** is something we should do.
At school our duties are to listen and to keep the classroom clean.

accessibility.textAlternative: A right is something every child should have, like being safe. A duty is something we should do, like listening.

content.body: Remember: a right is what you **should have**. A duty is what you **should do**.

items.prompt: Going to school. Right or duty?

feedback.correct: Yes! Every child should have school.
feedback.incorrect: School is something every child should have. That makes it a right.

optionFeedback: Yes! Every child should have school.
School is something every child should have. That makes it a right.

items.prompt: Picking up your rubbish. Right or duty?

feedback.correct: Yes! It is something we should do.
feedback.incorrect: Picking up rubbish is something we should do. That makes it a duty.

optionFeedback: Picking up rubbish is something we should do. That makes it a duty.
Yes! It is something we should do.

accessibility.textAlternative: Two read-aloud questions: is going to school, or picking up rubbish, a right or a duty?

offline.fallback: Can be played as stand-or-sit without a device.

items.prompt: Kollie walks near the road only when the teacher is looking. Is that good?

feedback.correct: Right! The rule keeps him safe all the time, not only when someone is watching.
feedback.incorrect: The road is dangerous even when nobody is looking. The rule keeps Kollie safe all the time.

optionFeedback: The road is dangerous even when nobody is looking. The rule keeps Kollie safe all the time.
Right! The rule keeps him safe all the time, not only when someone is watching.

items.prompt: Musu says, 'Sweets every day is my right.' Is it?

feedback.correct: Right! Sweets are a want. Being safe and going to school are rights.
feedback.incorrect: Sweets are nice, but a right is something every child needs, like being safe.

optionFeedback: Sweets are nice, but a right is something every child needs, like being safe.
Right! Sweets are a want. Being safe and going to school are rights.

accessibility.textAlternative: Two read-aloud yes-or-no questions about following a rule when nobody watches, and whether sweets are a right.

offline.fallback: Can be asked aloud without a device.

content.body: Your turn. Choose on your own.

items.prompt: 'Wash your hands before you eat.' Why do we have this rule?
options: To keep us healthy and safe
So the teacher can punish us

feedback.correct: Yes! Clean hands help stop sickness.
feedback.incorrect: Rules help us. This one keeps us healthy.

optionFeedback: Yes! Clean hands help stop sickness.
Rules help us. This one keeps us healthy.

items.prompt: Listening when a friend is talking. Right or duty?

feedback.correct: Yes! It is something we should do.
feedback.incorrect: Listening is something we should do. That is a duty.

optionFeedback: Listening is something we should do. That is a duty.
Yes! It is something we should do.

items.prompt: Being safe at school. Right or duty?

feedback.correct: Yes! Every child should be safe.
feedback.incorrect: Being safe is something every child should have. That is a right.

optionFeedback: Yes! Every child should be safe.
Being safe is something every child should have. That is a right.

accessibility.textAlternative: Three read-aloud questions: why we wash hands, and whether listening and being safe are rights or duties.

offline.fallback: Questions and feedback are saved with the lesson.

content.body: Say your answers. Your teacher can write them for you.

prompts.prompt: Tell one rule at home or school, and how it helps.
Tell one duty you have at school.

accessibility.textAlternative: Two spoken prompts: tell a rule and how it helps, and tell a duty at school.

offline.fallback: Answers are spoken; the teacher can write them on paper.

content.body: Your teacher will ask you to act out and tell. Do it on your own. Your teacher checks it, not this lesson.

accessibility.textAlternative: The teacher asks each child to act out a rule and tell a right and a duty.

offline.fallback: Your teacher asks you to act out a rule and to tell a right and a duty, then writes down what you show.

content.body:
What should Musu and Kollie do about the ball? Tell a partner.

Next week your teacher will ask about rules, rights and duties again.

accessibility.textAlternative: Tell a partner what the children should do about the ball; the topic returns next week.
